note: W1-LIBRARY round 3. The corpus was a clerical library: measured against per-skill vocabularies, axes-maces, greatweapons and shieldcraft scored ZERO across all 70 books, and polearms was single-book noise. A province with 87 named weapons and no written culture of arms is a seam showing. This file is the Imperial instructional spine of that culture — a regulation, a serjeant's marginalia answering it, an arms-master's treatise, a snob's letter that teaches the axe by despising it, and a bill-man's dictated reply. Two declared contradictions, both about method rather than about fact: whether a shield line may be opened in standing water, and whether a hooked weapon is fit for a soldier. Nothing adjudicates either. Sorcery was the last skill in game/data/progression/skills.json still scoring zero across the whole library after the martial expansion, and a battle-mage who has been told to stop asking for reagents is where an Imperial cohort's written culture of arms would actually keep it.

books.title: Standing Instruction for the Arming, Marching and Fighting of Auxiliary Cohorts in the Province of Black Marsh
books.author: Sixth issue, over the name of Legate Cassia Verano, Provincial Office at Gideon. Supersedes the fifth issue, which remains in force at Blackrose only
books.unreliability: Mostly right, and written by people who have actually buried men. Section 9 is the exception and it is lethal: the locked line is prescribed for standing water on the authority of a battle fought on a dry causeway, and the instruction forbids the one thing that saves the rank. No book in the game corrects it. A serjeant does, in the margin of his own copy, and he is disregarded.
books.wrong_on_purpose: Prescribes the three-rank locked shield line in standing water and forbids opening it, on the authority of an engagement fought on dry stone. The garrison bill section is sound, the axe section is sound, section 9 kills the second rank.

contradicts.on: whether the shield line may be opened in standing water

books.text:
STANDING INSTRUCTION FOR THE ARMING, MARCHING AND FIGHTING OF AUXILIARY COHORTS IN THE PROVINCE OF BLACK MARSH.

Sixth issue. To be held by every serjeant at the rank of file-leader and above. A cohort that has lost its copy is to apply to the Provincial Office at Gideon and is to be charged 8 drakes for the replacement.

1. WHAT THIS BOOK IS FOR.

The Legion has fought in this province for a long time and has written down almost nothing, because the men who learned the most about it did not come home to write. Five issues of this instruction were compiled in Cyrodiil by officers who had not served here. This one was compiled at Gideon by officers who had. Where the two disagree, this one is to be followed.

A recruit sent out from the interior of the Empire arrives believing three things, and all three will kill him. He believes the ground is ground. He believes an enemy out of sight is no enemy. He believes that when he is tired he may rest. Break him of the first in his first week, of the second in his first month, and of the third by making him march when he is tired, which is the only method that has ever worked.

2. THE ORDER OF ARMING.

Boots. Belt. Shield. Sword. Everything else afterwards, and if there is no time for everything else, there was never going to be.

A man who arms in that order can be in the line in under a minute from sleep. A man who begins with his cuirass will be found half-dressed and dead beside it. We've found several.

3. THE SHIELD.

The garrison kite is the arm of this cohort and it is the reason the cohort exists. Nothing else the Empire has brought to this province works as well as it does. A recruit who is issued one will complain of the weight for a month and will then refuse to be parted from it.

Learn its edges before you learn its face. The kite covers from the collarbone to below the knee and covers a shoulder's width to either side of the wrist, and a blow that arrives from outside that width does not glance off it. The blow lands as though the shield were on the other man's arm. There is a habit among recruits of raising the shield toward a shout — Left! Left! — and the shout is usually made by a man who intends to be shouting from the other side of you when the blow lands.

So: the shield is turned, not lifted. Turn from the hips. A recruit who learns to turn from the elbow will spend the rest of his service tiring in the first minute of every fight and blaming his rations.

4. THE SHIELD, CONTINUED. ON THE BOSS.

The face of the shield stops things. The rim and the boss do work. A shield used only to stop things is half a shield and its owner is half a soldier.

Drill the shove until it is done without thought. The shove is not a blow and it is not intended to hurt. It is intended to put a man's weight where his weight was not, and a man who has been moved half a pace has for a moment no arm to hit you with. That moment is your whole trade. Every serjeant reading this has watched a recruit shove a man beautifully and then stand admiring it.

5. THE SWORD.

The garrison sword is a short, plain, heavy-tipped blade and there is nothing to say about it that a month of drill will not say better. It is issued because it can be used badly by a tired man in a crowd without cutting the man beside him. That is its entire virtue and it is a considerable one.

The auxiliary who has grown up here will bring his own. Let him, within reason. A marsh-guard shortsword carried low and thrown from the hip is a real weapon in real hands and the men who carry them have been carrying them since they could walk. Do not issue a Kothringi bronze to anyone. They are handsome, they are old, and they bend.

6. THE BILL.

Every file is to carry 2 bills and they are to be given to the two largest men in it, not the two cleverest. The garrison bill hooks. Against a mounted man there is nothing better in the Empire's arsenal, and there are no mounted men here, so its use in this province is against boats, against a shield rim, and against the back of a knee.

Bill-men stand in the second rank and reach over the first. Their instruction is short and it is the same at every drill: *low, and pull*. A bill that goes in high has hit a shield and achieved nothing. A bill that goes in low has taken a man's leg out from under him and the first rank finishes what the second rank started.

7. THE AXE.

The Provincial Office issues no axes. Every cohort in this province carries them anyway and the Provincial Office is aware of it.

An officer newly arrived will want to stop this and should not. The auxiliary's shell-splitter is a wood-axe and a boat-axe and a shellfish tool and its owner has done ten thousand honest strokes with it before ever swinging it at a man. He does not need to be taught to use it. He needs to be taught not to swing it where his own file is standing, which is a different lesson and takes a day.

Where the axe earns its place is against a shield. A sword rings off a good shield all afternoon. An axe goes into the rim and stays there, and the man behind it must choose between his shield and his balance. The hatchets the marsh-guards carry near the head do not split a rim so much as hook it and drag it down, and a shield dragged down is a face uncovered.

8. THE GREAT WEAPONS.

No. Not in the line. A man swinging a claymore in a locked rank is a danger to four of his own and the Empire has paid for that lesson twice within living memory.

There is a place for them and it is outside the line: at a gate, in a lane, on a jetty, anywhere a single man must hold a width no two men can hold. Choose him for temperament and not for size. The great weapons punish a man who is frightened into hurrying, because they cannot be recalled once they are begun.

9. THE LINE IN WATER.

The cohort will frequently be required to hold a line in standing water. The instruction is the same as on dry ground and is to be followed as strictly.

Three ranks. Shields locked, rim over rim, the second rank's rim resting on the first rank's shoulder. The line does not open. Whatever comes at it, however it comes, the line does not open, and a file-leader who orders his file to open in water is to be broken to the ranks the same day.

The reasoning is set out in the fourth issue and has not been improved on since. At the Drowned Ford the line held for the better part of an afternoon against a force that was never counted, and it held because it did not open, and every account of that day agrees that the men who died were the men who broke rearward. Water is a discomfort. It is not a reason.

Officers will hear from local men that a rank standing in water above the knee cannot recover a man who has gone down, and that a locked line cannot let him up. This is true and it is not an argument for opening the line. It is an argument for not going down.

10. THE MARCH.

Twelve miles is a day here. An officer who plans on twenty will arrive with a cohort unfit to fight, and there is no fight in this province worth arriving to without a cohort that can fight.

Rest on the hour, in the water if there is nowhere dry, standing. A man who sits down in this country in wet boots does not get up the same man.

11. WHAT TO DO WHEN THEY ARE OUT OF SIGHT.

You will not usually see them. Accept it early. The auxiliaries you have recruited here can often see them and will not always say so, and an officer who punishes an auxiliary for being right is not going to be told again.

Halt. Face outward. Wait. This province has never once rewarded a cohort for hurrying and has repeatedly rewarded one for standing still and being boring to attack.

12. LAST.

Write down what happened. Write it even where it makes the cohort look poor, and especially where it makes you look poor, because five issues of this instruction were written by men who were guessing, and the guessing is what this issue exists to end.

13. BOATS.

More of this cohort's work happens in a boat than on a road and the Instruction has been silent on it through five issues, which is an embarrassment.

A punt with 6 men in it and their kit is at its limit. Put 8 in and it will float and it will not answer, and a boat that will not answer in a channel with a run on it is a coffin with a serjeant in it.

Kit in the middle, low, and lashed. Shields flat and not stacked upright, because a stacked shield takes wind like a sail and there is always more wind on water.

No man stands. Not to look, not to point, not because his legs have gone to sleep. A man standing in a punt is 12 stone at head height and the punt will do what it is told to do.

If she goes over: hold the boat. Not your kit, not your sword, not the man next to you. The boat floats and you do not, and everything else can be got again.

Every file is to contain one auxiliary who has poled since childhood and that auxiliary commands the boat, whatever his rank, and the officer aboard is a passenger and is to say so out loud in front of the men on the first day of every posting. An officer unwilling to say it will get the sentence read to him at his court.

14. THE WOUNDED.

Carry them. The Ninth does not leave men and has not left men in living memory and the day it does the whole arrangement this cohort has with this province comes apart.

Two men to a stretcher and change every 20 minutes, and 4 stretchers means 8 men out of your strength and a march at half speed and that is simply the cost.

A man hit in the belly is not to be given water however he asks and however you feel about refusing him.

A man who has gone into the water and been got out is to be stripped, dried and put between two others, in that order, and this applies in the wet season at noon and not only at night. Men have died of the cold in this province in a temperature no Nord would put a coat on for.

15. PRISONERS, AND WHAT IS TO BE DONE WITH PEOPLE FOUND INLAND.

The Cohort takes prisoners off boats and does not take prisoners inland, because the Cohort does not go inland.

A person found inland is not a prisoner and is not to be treated as one. They are to be spoken to, through an auxiliary and not through an officer's Tamrielic, and they are to be let alone, and whatever they say about where the column may and may not go is to be written down and reported and — this is the part every new officer resents — obeyed.

The Office is aware that this reads as an instruction to be turned back by unarmed people sitting on a rock. It is exactly that instruction. Six columns have disregarded it in 60 years and the Office is not able to say what became of two of them.

16. NIGHT.

Nothing moves at night in this province except by water and except in an emergency.

If you must: no lamps, no talking, one hand on the man in front, the poler leading, and a rope from the front man to the back man, tied and not held. Men who are holding a rope let go of it when something frightens them.

Halt at the first thing you do not understand and wait for light. A night halt that costs you 4 hours has never in the history of this cohort cost as much as a night march that went on.

17. THE AUXILIARIES.

Half the strength of this cohort was born in this province and every year that proportion rises, and the fifth issue of this Instruction contained no section about them at all.

They are soldiers of the Ninth. They are paid, fed, ranked and buried as soldiers of the Ninth and they are to be commanded as soldiers of the Ninth.

Three practical matters, since practical matters are what this book is for.

*They know the ground and you do not.* An officer who takes ground advice from an auxiliary loses nothing. An officer who overrules it should be able to answer one question afterwards, at his court: why?

*They have households 4 days away.* The standing order limiting posting distance is not sentiment, it is retention: the Cohort has tried it the other way and could not keep men. Do not apply for an exception. It will be refused and it will be remembered.

*They will not always tell you what they have seen.* This is section 11 and it bears repeating in its own place. An auxiliary who has been punished once for being right will be silent for the rest of his service, and the thing he is silent about will be the thing that kills your file.

18. SCHEDULE OF KIT, PER MAN, AS ISSUED AT GIDEON.

Sword, marsh or garrison pattern, 1. Shield, kite, 1. Helmet, 1. Cuirass, 1, and the Office is aware that it is not worn inland in the wet season and has decided not to see it. Boots, 2 pair, and this is the item on which the Cohort's whole effectiveness rests and the Office would rather be short of anything else. Pole, 1, cut locally. Blanket, oiled, 1. Rope, 20 feet, 1. Water bottle, 2 — two, not one, and a quartermaster who issues one is to be reported. Rations, 3 days.

Bills, 2 per file. Axes, 0, issued; see section 7.

SCHEDULE B. THE ARMS OF THE PROVINCE, FOR AN OFFICER WHO MUST RECOGNISE THEM.

Compiled at the request of the officer schools, which asked for a plate and have been sent words, the Office having no engraver.

An officer arriving here will be shown a great many weapons he has never seen and will make one of two errors. He will decide they are curiosities, or he will decide they are all the same thing. This schedule exists to prevent both. It is not a list of what the Cohort issues. It is a list of what will be in the hands of the people around you, on both sides, and what each one tells you about the person holding it.

*Knives, of shell and of bone.* Universal. Every household in this province has one and it is a tool. A drawn knife here means very little and an officer who reacts to one has told the whole landing what he is. The exception is the hooked root-thorn, which is drawn back through a wound rather than out of it, and which is not a tool, and which is never carried by accident.

*The claw and the bound fist.* Worn, not carried. Never taken at a gate, and absent from every search. Assume that a person in this province who appears to be unarmed is within their rights to be, and that a proportion of them are not unarmed.

*Curved blades, two patterns.* The long shallow sickle sweeps and lives at a distance. The short deep reaver chops and lives close. They are made on the same coast and they are opposite weapons, and an officer who has learned to read which one a man is carrying has learned how that man intends to fight before anything has happened.

*Straight swords.* Ours and theirs. The marsh pattern is shorter than the garrison sword and is carried low on the left and is thrown from the hip. Half this cohort carries it. It is a good sword.

*Thrusting swords.* Imported, expensive, and found at Gideon and Archon in the hands of gentlemen and of the people gentlemen employ. Almost never seen inland. A thrusting sword more than a day from a customs house is a thing to think about.

*Spears, two holds.* Underhand and braced at the hip, which is the weir hold, and overhand from above the shoulder, which is the boat hold. Both are gigs and both are fishing tools and both will go through a cuirass. This is the commonest weapon in the province by a very large margin and no Imperial account of the province has ever said so.

*Bills, hooks and glaives.* Ours mostly, and the hooks are in the hands of every man who has ever cut brush. Long, slow, no defence in them, and they take the legs.

*Axes and the short hatchets.* Tools. See section 7. Assume every adult in a coastal settlement can use one competently, because every adult in a coastal settlement does use one, daily, on shell.

*Maces and the cast heads.* Cheap, local, ugly and effective, and made in quantity because the iron here will not hold an edge. A village that has armed itself in a hurry has armed itself with these.

*The chain.* Rare, and carried on quays and in holds. Do not stand next to one.

*The great weapons.* Two-handed blades and the long curved reaping blades of the drowned processions. The reaping blades are a duty and not usually a weapon, and the Cohort's standing courtesy is that we do not remark on them and do not ask to see one, and the courtesy has been kept for 60 years and has cost the Empire nothing.

*Bows.* Horn-and-sinew in the dry season, chitin recurve all year, reed shortbow everywhere. Effective range in this country is short — the sight lines are not there — and an officer who has been shot at from 40 paces has been shot at by a hunter who chose the ground.

*The great shields, called doors.* Carried at Helstrom and at the deep settlements and almost never seen on the coast. Three of them abreast will stop a lane. They cannot turn a blow aside and do not attempt it, and a party that meets 3 of them has met people who intend to protect the ones behind them and not people who intend to attack, and should conduct itself accordingly.

**A closing word to the officer this schedule was written for.** Nothing above is exotic. Every weapon in it is a working tool that its owner has been holding since childhood, and the reason they are dangerous is not that they are strange but that they are ordinary. You are not facing an armoury. You are facing a province in which the population is competent, and in which almost every person's daily work has already taught them the stroke.

books.title: What Is Written in the Back of Serjeant Attus Brell's Sixth Issue
books.author: Attus Brell, file-leader and then serjeant, Ninth Cohort, 22 years, most of them wet
books.unreliability: He is right about section 9 and he cannot prove it, and he knows he cannot prove it, and he says so. He is also comprehensively wrong about the bill, which he has disliked since a bill-man dropped one on his foot at Thorn, and he never mentions the foot.

contradicts.on: whether the shield line may be opened in standing water

books.text:
I've kept this book 9 years and I've never written in it and I'm writing in it now because Verano's dead and can't be argued with any other way.

The rest of it is good. I want that down first. Sections 1 through 8 are the best writing the Legion has ever done about this province and I would put a copy in the hand of every recruit who came off the boat if the Office would pay for it. The bit about arming in order — boots, belt, shield, sword — I have used that on every recruit I ever had and I have never lost one half-dressed. The bit about not punishing an auxiliary for being right, that's worth the whole book on its own.

Section 9 is going to keep killing men and I can't make them listen.

Here is what it says. Three ranks, locked, and the line does not open, and a file-leader who opens it goes back to the ranks that day. Here's what actually happens.

Water above the knee. Doesn't need to be deep. Knee-deep and a bit of a run on it. First rank's got the whole weight of the second rank's rim on his shoulder and he's braced forward into it because that's the drill. Something hits the line hard, or the bottom goes soft under one man, or he just tires — and he goes down. Now. He's under. He's a foot under and he's got 60 pounds of kit on and there's a shield rim across the back of his neck holding him there, and it's OUR shield rim, and the man holding it can't lift it without breaking the lock, and breaking the lock is what Verano says gets you broken to the ranks.

I have watched it four times. Twice I opened and got him up and got shouted at. Twice I did not.

Do you want to know what the difference was? The difference was who was standing behind me.

Now the Ford. They all quote the Ford at me. The line held at the Ford, the line did not open at the Ford, the men who died at the Ford were the ones who broke rearward. Has any officer who says it to me ever asked what the bottom was made of?

I was not at the Ford. I have talked to 3 men who were, and here is the thing that has never been put in the book. It is a ford. It is a stone causeway. There is a reason people cross the river at that place and not at another one. The water was over their boots and not over their knees and the bottom under them was Kothringi cut stone that does not go soft. Verano took a rule that was true on a paved crossing and wrote it down for a swamp.

I have said this to 2 officers and both of them told me the same thing, and it was not that I was wrong. It was that if the instruction says the line may open at the file-leader's discretion, then every frightened file-leader in the province opens the line, and then you have not got a line at all, you have 300 men standing in water on their own. And I know that. I do know that. I have seen a line come apart and it is the worst thing I have ever seen and it takes about 4 seconds.

So I'm not asking for discretion. I'm asking for a WORD. Give me a word to shout that means *the man in the second rank lifts his rim off the first rank's shoulder and nothing else moves*. Not open. Lift. The lock stays, the front stays, the feet stay, the rim comes up 8 inches and the drowning man gets his head out and the whole thing takes as long as it takes to say it.

You could drill it in a morning. I have drilled it in a morning, with my own file, in the wet season, against the instruction, and if any officer wants to charge me for it he can find me at Gideon and I will show him the drill first.

While I'm in here.

The bill. Section 6 says give the bills to the two largest men in the file. Rubbish. Give them to the two men who do not get excited. A big man with a bill in a crowd is 8 feet of hook going through the space where your own second rank keeps its faces. I have had my helmet taken off my head from behind by one of ours and I have never once been hooked by one of theirs. The bill is a fine thing on a jetty and a menace in a rank, and Verano loved it because he saw it work once at a boat and never had to stand next to one.

The axe section is right. I would only add: teach them the rim. Every recruit who picks up a hatchet wants to hit the man. The man is behind a shield. Hit the shield's edge where it is thin, hook it, drag it down and let the fellow beside you put his sword in the gap you made. Two men and one axe is worth six men and no axe, and I have never got that into the instruction either.

And the great weapons. Section 8 says choose for temperament, not size, and that is the best sentence in the book and I have never seen an officer obey it. They always give the big sword to the big lad. The big lad is 19 and he is frightened and he starts his swing early and then he's got 5 feet of steel going round and he can't stop it and he can't get it back, and the fellow he is swinging at has already stepped inside it. Give it to the slow one. Give it to the one who is boring. I gave one to a fenland lad from Blackrose who never said a word in 3 years and he held a lane at Stormhold on his own for as long as it took us to get the boats off, and he did it by not swinging until it was worth swinging.

I'm going to put this book back on the shelf now and I don't expect it to be read.

If you're reading it and you're a serjeant: LIFT! Don't open. Lift the rim, get him up, and if they break you for it, they break you for it.

While I am in here I will do the rest of it.

SECTION 10, THE MARCH. Twelve miles. Right. Never argue with 12 miles. I have had 3 officers try 16 and all 3 of them arrived with a cohort that could not have fought a duck, and 2 of them wrote it up as a successful march because they had got there.

Rest standing on the pole. Right again, and it is the hardest order in the book to give, because a tired man looks at you as though you have hit him. Give it anyway. I have never had a man stiffen up on me.

SECTION 11, WHEN YOU CAN'T SEE THEM. Best section in the book, and Verano knew it, because it's the only one where he stops telling you what to do and tells you what not to do.

Halt. Face outward. Wait. I have done that 6 times in 22 years and 6 times nothing happened, and the 6 times nothing happened are why I am writing in a book instead of lying in the river.

And the bit about not punishing an auxiliary for being right — I want to put something down about that, because Verano wrote it as a piece of good sense and it is not. It is the whole of how this cohort works.

I had a lad, Ganeeth, came in at 17, could not read, could swim like an otter. Third year, we are going up the north channel and he says to me, quiet, not in front of the file: serjeant, that water has come up and it should not have. I said how do you know that? He said I don't know how I know.

Now. I could have said don't be soft. That's what my serjeant would have said to me.

I said all right and I halted and we sat there like fools for 2 hours and then the whole channel came down black with the top of a weir in it.

He's a decurion now. He's the third Argonian decurion the Ninth's ever had and he's got a file of his own and he'll be a serjeant when I'm gone, and the reason I've got him is that I said all right that day instead of don't be soft.

That's not in any book. Verano got closest and even he made it sound like manners.

SECTION 12, WRITE IT DOWN. Yes. And I will say the thing he would not.

The reason five issues of this book were rubbish is that the men who knew got killed and the men who wrote it did not. That's it. One sentence, and it is the whole of the reason. A man who has been out here 20 years has forgotten more about this province than the Office has ever written down, and then they die at 50 of the rot and it goes with them.

I have been asked twice to write a book proper and both times I have said I am not a writer, and both times that was a lie, and what I actually meant was that the press at Gideon would not print a serjeant.

ON VERANO HIMSELF, SINCE HE'S DEAD AND CAN'T MIND.

He came out to Thorn once. Stood in the yard in the rain for 3 hours watching my file drill and did not say a word and every man of us was terrified.

At the end he came over and asked me one question. He said: what would you take out of it?

I said section 9.

He looked at me for a long time and then he said: so would I, and I can't.

And then he got in his boat.

I have thought about that for 9 years and I still do not know what he meant. Could he not do it because of the Office? Because he could think of nothing to put in its place? Or because striking it out meant saying in print that the Ninth was never in a battle at the Ford at all? Probably all 3.

He was a decent man and he wrote a good book and section 9 is going to keep killing people, and both of those are true, and I have never been able to hold them in my head at the same time for longer than about a minute.

LIFT. Don't open.

books.title: On the Hanging Guard, and Against the New Grip
books.author: Berethun Cray, arms-master, formerly of the Chorrol schools, now teaching at Gideon to whoever will pay
books.unreliability: He teaches the greatsword very well and he is dead wrong about why the Nord grip is winning. He has decided it is a fashion and a decadence; it is a mechanical advantage he has never tested, because he will not hold a sword that way for long enough to find out.
books.wrong_on_purpose: Argues the high grip on the ricasso is a decadence that trades reach for showmanship. It trades reach for turnover, and the men beating him with it know that and he has not asked them.

contradicts.on: whether the high grip on the ricasso is worth the reach it gives up

books.text:
A word to the young gentleman who has bought a greatsword because he saw one carried through Gideon on a feast day.

Do you know what you have bought? You have bought a lever. You have not bought a sword. Until you understand the difference you will be beaten by boys with hatchets, and you will believe you were unlucky, and you will buy a bigger one.

THE FIRST THING.

Everything a greatsword does, it does by going round. It has no small motions. A shortsword has a dozen little corrections in it; a greatsword has none, and every stroke you begin is a promise you have made to the ground and to the man in front of you and you will keep it whether you like the outcome or not.

Therefore the whole art is in the *choosing*, and hardly any of it is in the swinging. A man who swings well and chooses badly is a mill-wheel. I have taught a great many mill-wheels. Some of them are dead now and I am sorry about it and I told them.

THE HANGING GUARD.

Point down and to the left, hands high, hilt at the level of your own ear, the blade lying along the outside of your leading leg like a gate that has been left ajar.

Nine tenths of what I teach is this position and how to leave it.

Why: from the hanging guard every stroke you own is already half made. The weight is up where you want it and gravity is on your side for the whole first half of the arc, and gravity is the only ally a greatsword has that never tires. From the high guard, hands above the head, you are stronger and you are slower and you are advertising. From the low guard you are quick to the legs and you have nothing at all for a man who comes at your head.

How to leave it: you do not lift out of the hanging guard. You *drop*. The hands come down and inward and the point comes up and over and round, and if you have done it correctly the sword has gone from your left ankle to the other man's collarbone without once passing through a position from which you could have been read.

Practise it against a post until the post is ashamed. Then practise it against a post while walking backwards through water, because you are in Black Marsh and not one opponent in this province has ever had the courtesy to fight you on a floor.

WHAT THE GREATSWORD IS ACTUALLY FOR.

Width. Not strength. Everyone says strength and everyone is repeating what their father said.

A greatsword is for holding a width that two men could not hold, and it does this because the arc is long enough that a man has no way into your ground without crossing it somewhere. Put a competent greatsword in a doorway, on a jetty, at the head of a stair, and you have shut it. Put the same man in an open field against three and he will be killed from the side by the second one while he is still finishing his promise to the first.

So: doorways, lanes, gangplanks, the top of a ladder, the mouth of a bridge. There is no other employment for it. Learn to read a ground for its narrow places the way a poler reads water. If you can't find a narrow place, make one, and if you can't make one, put the thing on your back and pick up something else, and do not be proud about it.

AGAINST THE NEW GRIP.

I come now to a thing that has been irritating me for 6 years.

There is a fashion, brought down from the north by way of the Blackwood and taken up with enthusiasm by young men at Gideon who ought to know better, of holding the greatsword with the leading hand *above the guard*, on the flat of the blade itself, where the edge has been left blunt for a span. They call it the high grip. The Nords who brought it call it something I will not write.

Consider what has been given up. You have shortened your own weapon by the length of your forearm. You have thrown away the reach that is the sword's only unanswerable argument. You have put your bare hand out in front of the crossguard, which exists, I remind the reader, to stop things arriving at your hand.

And what has been bought? Speed, they say. It turns over faster, they say. Faster than what, and measured by whom?

It looks faster. I grant that. A shorter lever always looks faster, and a young man who has been beaten by something that looked fast will tell you it was fast. But a stroke that arrives at the collarbone in less time from closer in has not travelled faster; it has travelled less far. You may achieve the same by standing nearer, which costs you nothing and does not require you to hold your sword as though you were carrying a plank up a stair.

I have said this in the yard at Gideon and I have said it in print and I have twice been asked to demonstrate. I decline, and I will say plainly why I decline, because the young men have been saying I am afraid. I decline because I am 61, and because a demonstration proves what the two men in it can do and not what the method can do, and because the fen lads who fight this way are 25 and have arms like cables and would beat me holding the sword by the point.

Let them win their bouts. The method is a fashion and fashions go. When they are 40 and their wrists have gone they will hold the sword by the handle like their grandfathers, and they will come to me and I will not say anything, and they will know.

LAST, AND THIS IS FREE.

If you are ever in a lane with a greatsword and a man comes at you fast with something short: do not swing.

Step back once, keep the hanging guard, and let him come to a stop. He has to stop. The lane will not let him past you and he can't live inside your arc for longer than a breath. He will stop, and he will be close, and he will be thinking about how close he is.

Then drop.

THE FOUR STROKES, WHICH ARE ALL OF THEM.

I am often asked how many strokes I teach and the young men are disappointed by the answer.

*The drop.* Hanging guard to the collarbone, described above. This is 6 of every 10 strokes you will ever throw and it should be 8.

*The rising cut.* From the same guard, but the point goes out and up rather than over, arriving under the arm or at the inside of the elbow. Its use is against a man who has learned to expect the drop, and its use is therefore entirely against people who have been watching you, which in this province means people who have been watching you for some time from somewhere you did not know about.

*The half-sword thrust.* Left hand leaves the grip and takes the blade above the guard — and yes, I am aware of what I have written elsewhere in this book about hands on blades, and no, I do not consider it the same thing, because I am doing it for one motion and not living there. Point into a gap, both hands driving. It is the only thing a greatsword owns that works at a range shorter than its own length.

*The winding.* When two great weapons have met and neither has gone through, do not withdraw. Whoever withdraws first gives the other man a free stroke. Keep the pressure, walk your point around his, and come off the far side of his blade into whatever he has left uncovered. Pupils find this the hardest thing in the school and it is the only thing that has ever saved me.

Four. There is no fifth, and there has never needed to be. A man who can do 4 things without thinking beats a man who can do 20 with thinking, and I have never once in 40 years seen that proposition fail.

AGAINST A SHIELD.

Do not hit the shield! I have to say it at every intake and I will be saying it again in a fortnight.

A greatsword against a good shield is 2 tired men and a noise. The shield covers a wedge and the wedge has edges, and the whole of your work is to make him move it and then to be somewhere else.

Threaten low. He drops. Go over the top with the drop and take the shoulder or the side of the neck.

Or: take the shield's rim with the point on the way past and drag it across him, which is the axeman's trick borrowed, and I am not too proud to borrow it and neither should you be.

Or, and this is the one they never expect from a man with 5 feet of steel: half-sword and put the point into his foot. He will move the foot. Everything above the foot comes with it.

AGAINST A SPEAR, WHICH IS WHAT YOU WILL ACTUALLY MEET HERE.

You will lose this one more often than you win it and I want that understood before the method.

A spearman with sense keeps you at the end of his shaft and walks backwards, and there is no answer to a man walking backwards except being faster than him or having somewhere for him to walk into.

The method, such as it is: beat the shaft aside with the flat, hard, and go in on the beat and not after it. One beat, one step, and you are either inside the point or you are dead, and a man who beats and then thinks about it has beaten the shaft aside for nothing because a shaft comes back.

Never beat downward. A spear beaten downward is a spear at your knee. Beat across.

ON A PUPIL OF MINE.

I taught a young man at Gideon 4 years ago whose name I will not print because his mother is alive.

He was the best natural hand I have had in 20 years in this province. He had the drop at 3 months. He could wind at a year, which I could not do at 5.

He went out to a matter at the customs house yard against a man with a duelling pick and he was killed on the second exchange, and the reason he was killed is that he stood on ground he had not looked at, and his back foot went in, and everything I had ever taught him assumed a floor.

I have written a great deal in this book about doorways and jetties and the tops of stairs, and I put it in because of him, and every intake I say it and every intake at least one young man thinks I am being tiresome about ground.

Look at the ground. Look at it before you agree to be there. It's the only lesson in this book you don't get a second offer of.

books.title: The Axe in the Hand of a Fool: A Letter to a Nephew Who Has Been Seduced
books.author: Corvus Lentulus Balbo, of the Anvil salle, uncle
books.unreliability: Every fact in it is accurate. Every conclusion drawn from those facts is snobbery. He describes axe-work better than anyone else in the library because he has studied it carefully in order to be rude about it, and a reader who ignores the last line of every paragraph has been taught the weapon by a man who would be horrified.
books.wrong_on_purpose: Holds that the axe is beneath a gentleman and loses to a sword in any honest exchange. His own worked examples show the axe winning, and he attributes each win to the swordsman's error rather than to the weapon.

contradicts.on: whether a hooked weapon is fit for a soldier

books.text:
Nephew,

Your mother writes that you have sold the sword I gave you at your naming and bought an axe, and that you are pleased with yourself, and that you have been telling the household at dinner that the axe is the honest weapon of the province and the sword is a decoration.

I am going to answer this properly, because you are 20 and because a badly answered enthusiasm at 20 becomes a settled opinion at 30, and I would rather spend an evening's paper than have a nephew who thinks like a bargeman. A bargeman, Aulus!

FIRST, LET ME SAY WHAT IS TRUE, SO YOU MAY NOT ACCUSE ME OF NOT KNOWING.

The axe is a real weapon. I have watched it kill men. I have watched it kill men who were better swordsmen than the men holding the axes, and I have thought carefully about why, and here is why.

An axe puts all of its weight in the last hand's breadth of itself. A sword spreads its weight along a yard of steel. Two men of equal strength swing, and the axe arrives with everything it has in one place, and the sword arrives with a fraction of what it has spread along an edge. Against anything hard, the axe wins the exchange. Against a shield in particular it does not glance and it does not ring; it goes in, and it stops, and it stays.

This is the whole matter and everything else about the axe follows from it. Write it in your book if you keep one.

Now: because it goes in and stays, the axe is a weapon of *engagement* and not of *touching*. A swordsman may touch a man and withdraw and the exchange is over. An axeman who lands has bound himself to whatever he has landed in. If he has landed in a shield he now has the shield. If he has landed in a man he now has to get it back.

The good ones — and I concede they exist — have made this their advantage rather than their difficulty. They *intend* to catch the shield. They do not aim at the middle of it, where it is strong and where a hit achieves nothing but a bruise; they aim at the rim, low and near, where the wood is thin and the leather turns the corner. The head goes over the edge and the beard of it bites the back, and now the axeman has a grip on the other man's shield with the whole weight of his shoulders behind it, and he pulls it down and outward.

Do you see what has happened? I want you to notice it, because it is the cleverest thing in the trade and it was not invented by gentlemen.

Nothing has been cut. No blood has been drawn. And the swordsman's shield is now at his waist and his face is uncovered, and he has one of two choices: keep the shield and be hit in the face, or drop the shield and be a man with no shield in front of a man with an axe. There is no third choice. The axeman has taken away the thing that was making the fight even, and he has done it with a tool he uses for splitting firewood.

The short hatchets they carry in the marsh are worse — I mean better, and I decline to correct the pen. Held near the head, they are quicker than they have any right to be, they hook a rim rather than splitting it, and a man with one in each hand can take a shield down with the left and open you with the right in the time it takes a swordsman to think about his footing.

I have seen this done to a friend of mine at Stormhold by a fenland auxiliary who could not write his own name. My friend was the better fencer by a distance. Do you know where he is? He is buried at Stormhold.

SO WHY, THEN, IS THE AXE STILL BENEATH YOU?

Because everything I have just described is a *trick*, and a trick works until it is known.

Note that the axeman must land. Note that he must land on a particular part of a particular thing. Note that if he misses the rim and takes the face of the shield he has spent his whole swing to make a noise, and that he is now open for as long as it takes to bring the head back up, which is longer than it takes a swordsman to do anything he likes. The axe has no small motions. It has no recovery. It commits, absolutely, every time, and a man who commits absolutely against a man who does not is a man who will be beaten by patience.

The sword makes no promises. That is its refinement and it is why gentlemen carry it. A swordsman may begin a cut and change his mind halfway and end in a thrust; may touch, withdraw, touch again; may spend an afternoon learning an opponent at no cost. The axeman is buying every question he asks and paying the full price whether the answer is any good or not.

Your fenland auxiliary beat my friend because my friend fought him as though he were a fencer. He was not a fencer. He was a man with one question, and my friend answered it, and my friend was standing in the wrong place when he answered it.

I do not blame the axe for that. I blame my friend, who was careless, and who had been careless at Anvil too, where it cost him nothing.

CONCLUSION, AND THEN I WILL LET YOU ALONE.

Carry your axe. I would rather a nephew who has chosen a weapon and studied it than one who wears a sword because it goes with the coat.

But understand what you have chosen. You have chosen a weapon that will win you every fight against a man who does not know it and lose you every fight against a man who does. You have chosen to be a question and not an argument. And when you are 40, and your shoulder has gone, and committing the way this weapon requires 200 times is beyond you in an afternoon, you will find that the sword is still there and still does not require anything of you that is beyond giving.

Your mother says you are happy. I am glad of it. Come at harvest and bring the axe and we will see.

Your uncle,
CORVUS

*P.S. — Do not, whatever else you do, buy a flail. There are men in this province who will tell you a chain is the same idea carried further. It is not carried further. It is carried past the point at which you can get it back.*

---

A SECOND LETTER, WRITTEN A FORTNIGHT AFTER THE FIRST, AND SENT WITH IT.

Nephew,

I have had your answer and I have read it twice and I am going to concede two things and then take back rather more than I concede.

You say I have written 900 words on how to defeat a shield with an axe in the course of proving that the axe is beneath you, and that this is a strange way to be contemptuous of something.

Fair. I have thought about it. I studied the thing in order to be rude about it and I studied it properly because I do not know how to study a thing improperly, and the consequence is that a boy of 20 now has the best account of axe-work in the province in a letter from a man who thinks it is for bargemen. Take it. It cost you nothing and it cost me a fortnight.

You say further that I have not accounted for the two-handed axe, and here you have caught me and I will pay.

THE TWO-HANDED AXE, WHICH I OMITTED.

I omitted it because everything I said about the one-handed axe is *more* true of it and the argument would have been dull.

It commits harder. It recovers slower. It is unanswerable against anything it lands on and it is a liability for as long as it is travelling, and the whole art of using one is the art of choosing a moment, exactly as I described, only with a longer penalty for choosing wrong.

But I will add the one thing that is genuinely different, because you will meet it here and I would rather you met it having read this.

A two-handed axe does not need to hit a man to beat him. It only needs to hit his weapon.

A sword that has been struck by 8 pounds of iron at the end of a 4-foot lever does not stay in the line it was in. It may not stay in the hand. And a swordsman whose blade has been knocked across his own body is, for that instant, a man wearing his own weapon like a scarf. The good axemen here open with that, deliberately, as their first stroke, and they do not aim at you at all.

The counter, since you will want one, is not to be there. Do not meet it. Let the weight go past and come in behind it. Everything I told you about patience applies double.

WHAT I WILL NOT CONCEDE.

You say the sword is a gentleman's affectation and that a weapon should be judged by whether it wins.

Then judge it. Go to any yard in the Empire and put a good swordsman against a good axeman 20 times, on a floor, with edges blunted and a judge, and count.

You will not do this, because you know the answer, and because the answer is boring: the sword wins on a floor and the axe wins in the mud and neither of those is a fact about virtue.

Here is the sentence I actually want you to have, and it has taken me two letters to arrive at it, and I am not going to pretend I had it at the start.

*Every weapon is an argument about where you expect to be standing.*

The rapier is an argument that you will be on a floor with one other person and a great deal of notice. The garrison sword is an argument that you will be shoulder to shoulder with people it would be ruin to cut. The axe is an argument that the man in front of you will have a shield and that you will get exactly one chance at it. The flail is an argument that there will be no room at all. And your fenland auxiliary at Stormhold, who could not write his name, had made his argument correctly and my friend had made his in Anvil.

So carry the axe. You have chosen the province's argument, and you are in the province.

Only do not come home in 10 years and tell me it is the honest weapon and the sword is a decoration, because you will have started saying it to annoy me and you will have ended up believing it, and a man who believes his tools are virtuous has stopped looking at the ground.

Your uncle,
CORVUS

*P.S. — I meant what I said about the flail and I have since been told that a serjeant on the Gideon quays has written a whole book defending it. I would read it. I would not stand next to him.*

books.title: An Answer to the Gentleman From Anvil, Written by One of the Hooking Sort
books.author: Dag Ostrey, bill-man, Ninth Cohort, dictated to the cohort clerk at Thorn because he does not write
books.unreliability: He answers an argument he has heard secondhand in an alehouse and misremembers half of it, and he is right anyway. He also thinks the letter was about him. It was not about him.

contradicts.on: whether a hooked weapon is fit for a soldier

books.text:
A gentleman's letter about the axe has got into the province and men have been reading bits of it out at Thorn for a fortnight and laughing, and one of them read out the bit about the hooking sort being no fit weapon for a soldier, and everyone looked at me.

So. I'm the hooking sort. I've carried a bill 14 years. Write this down as I say it, Neveni, don't tidy it.

The gentleman says a hook is a trick, and a trick works until it is known. Right. Everything is a trick until it is known. His sword is a trick. The first man who ever put a point on a stick was doing a trick, and every man he did it to thought it was very unfair.

Here is what I know about the bill, and I will tell it straight, and some of it goes against me.

WHAT IT'S GOOD FOR.

It is good for the second rank. It is good for nothing else. Any officer who has put me anywhere but the second rank has been an officer I had to work around.

You stand behind your mate. Your mate has the shield and he has the whole business of being frightened, and you've got 8 feet of ash with a hook and a spike and a bit of an edge, and you are looking over his shoulder at the man opposite, and you are not looking at the man's face. Never look at the face. Look at his front knee.

Then: low, and pull. That's the whole of it. Everything else is decoration. Low, and pull.

You put the hook past his shield — under it, round it, over the top of it if he is a tall one and lazy — and you get it behind the knee or the ankle and you don't chop, you PULL, and you sit down into it with your whole weight like a man hauling a boat in.

He goes down. He always goes down. A man standing in mud cannot be pulled and stay standing. What is his foot supposed to argue with? And a man on his back in a fight is finished, and your mate in the front rank does the finishing, and neither of you has done anything a gentleman would call fencing.

ON WHAT IT IS AND WHAT IT ISN'T.

They call it a halberd in the Empire. In the stores at Gideon it is written down as a halberd. It is not one. A halberd has an axe head on it and a spike on top and it was made for a man on a horse. Where are the horses? What we carry is a bill: a hedging tool with a hook and a bit of a spike, on a longer pole than a hedger would want, made for cutting brush, and it does that better than it does this.

Same family as the spear, and I will say the honest thing about the spear too. A spear is a better weapon than a bill in every way but one. It is quicker. It is simpler. You can teach it to a farmer in an afternoon, and a wall of spears will stop anything that has ever walked. The marsh-lance the auxiliaries throw down overhand from above the shoulder is a lovely thing and I could not do it if I trained until I was 50.

The one way the bill is better: a spear can only push. A bill can pull. The whole difference between the two weapons is in that one word, and it is why I carry one and not the other, and if you take nothing else from this, take that a hook is a spear working in the other direction.

The glaive the marsh-guards carry is a third thing again — all blade, no hook, and it cuts down a lane where a bill sweeps across one. Beautiful weapon. Wrong weapon for standing behind your mate.

WHAT IT'S BAD FOR.

Everything else. And I will say it before some clever officer says it for me.

It is no good on your own. No man ever won a fight alone with a bill. If you are alone with one, drop it. Run. Pick up whatever is on the ground. It has no defence in it. It is slow to bring back. It is 8 feet of nuisance in a doorway. And in a crowd it will take your own mate's ear off, and I have done that, and I would rather have been hit myself.

Serjeant Brell says give the bills to the men who don't get excited, not the big ones. Brell is right. Brell has been saying it for years. The officers do not listen, because a bill looks like a big man's tool. It is not. It is a patient man's tool. You stand there and you do nothing for a long time. You do nothing while your mate is being hit. You do nothing while you are being shouted at. And then his front knee comes forward 6 inches and you take it and you sit down.

ON BEING A COWARD.

That's the real complaint, isn't it? Not that it does not work. That it works and it is not brave.

I have thought about it. I have. You stand behind another man and you hit people who are not looking at you.

Only — here is the thing the ones who say it have never done. Stand in the second rank for one afternoon and see how it feels to be the man who cannot cover himself. I have no shield. I have both hands on a pole. Everything that comes over the top comes to me and I can do nothing about any of it, and I cannot step back because there is a third rank behind me, and I cannot step forward because there is Brell. I stand there and hold my mate's life in my hands and hope my mate is holding mine.

If that's cowardice, it's a strange sort of cowardice where you are the one who cannot defend himself.

ONE MORE THING AND THEN I'M DONE, NEVENI.

The gentleman's letter says the axe is a question and the sword is an argument. I liked that. I would only say he has put the bill in the wrong place, because the bill is not a question OR an argument.

The bill is the ground. The bill takes the ground away from him. He can be as clever as he likes about where his sword is going while he is sitting in the water.

That's what I want said. Now read it back, and if you've made me sound clever, take it out!

books.title: Notes on the Employment of Destructive Magic in This Province, Submitted by an Officer Who Has Been Asked to Stop Applying for Reagents
books.author: Battle-Mage Tertius Ollo, attached to the Ninth Cohort at Gideon for nine years, unattached since
books.unreliability: A first-rate practical account of what destructive magic actually does in a wet, close, green country, written by a man who has diagnosed everything except himself. He believes the province defeated his craft. His craft was taught to him on a hill in Cyrodiil and every one of his failures is a failure of a method that assumes the caster can see.
books.wrong_on_purpose: Concludes that the climate is what makes destructive sorcery unworkable here. The reagents, the fire, the shock and the frost all behave exactly as he describes; what fails, in every one of his own worked examples, is that he never had line of sight, and he never once names it.

contradicts.on: whether a caster in this province can be relied on to see what he is casting at

books.text:
The Provincial Office has replied to my fourth application for a reagent allowance by observing that the Ninth Cohort has managed for sixty years without a battle-mage, that it will manage for sixty more, and that I might consider whether the fault lies in the allowance.

I have considered it for a year, and this is what I have to say, and it is longer than they will want.

I. WHAT A BATTLE-MAGE IS TRAINED TO DO.

The schools at the Imperial City produce a wizard who can put a destructive spell into a body at eighty paces, three or four times before he is spent, and who can do it while being shot at. The employment is that and nothing else, and everything else the schools teach — the wards, the enchantment of a serjeant's blade before an action, the small conjuration that fetches a rope across a river — is decoration hung upon that one competence.

I could do it at twenty-four, on a hill above Bruma, into a straw man at eighty paces, four times in a morning, and my instructors wrote a letter about me which I still have.

II. WHAT HAPPENS TO THAT MAN WHEN YOU PUT HIM IN A MARSH.

*The fire will not carry.* Every destructive spell in the Imperial curriculum below the fourth tier is some arrangement of fire, and fire in this air behaves as though it has been asked to do something impolite. It goes out. It does not go out at once, which would at least be honest; it arrives, it takes, it gutters, and the man it has arrived at beats it off his sleeve with a wet hand and comes on. I have set fire to a boat twice in nine years and both boats were dry and both were on the coast.

*The frost is worse and I did not expect it to be.* A frost spell works by taking the heat out of a thing quickly, and it is magnificent in dry cold country where a man's own body has nothing to spare. Here every surface is already carrying water, and the water takes the spell instead of the man, and what you have produced at the end of a great expenditure is a wet soldier who is briefly colder and considerably more awake.

*The shock alone is honest.* It is the one school that works in this province and it works better than it works anywhere else, for reasons any fisher caught out in a channel in a storm can supply without a lecture. I have used it four times in earnest and it has done everything the schools promised and rather more than I wanted on one occasion at Stormhold, and I do not intend to write that occasion down.

III. THE REAGENTS, WHICH IS WHERE THE OFFICE AND I HAVE FALLEN OUT.

A wizard of the Imperial schools carries powders, and the powders rot.

The quarrel is that, entire, and I have put it in four applications in increasingly plain language. Fire-salts cake and lose their virtue within a season in this air, and the sealed jars the Office issues are sealed against dust and were never designed against a climate that is trying to get in. My allowance is calculated at the rate paid at Chorrol, where a jar of salts lasts a wizard three years, and I am asking for the rate of a man who loses one every four months, and the Office has replied to me each time as though I were asking for a larger dinner. A larger dinner!

I want to record, because it will otherwise be forgotten, that the local practitioners have no such difficulty, and that I have asked why, and that the answer given to me by a rootkeeper at Helstrom was a question of her own. Where do you keep yours, she said, when you are not using it? In a sealed jar, I said, and I described the jar. She thought about that for a while. Then it's in the jar with the weather, she said, and would not say anything further, and I have not been able to get past that sentence in a year of thinking about it.

IV. THE ONE ADVANTAGE, WHICH I HAVE NOT BEEN ABLE TO PERSUADE ANY OFFICER TO USE.

Enchantment does not care about the weather.

A blade taken to a wizard before an action and given a shock enchantment holds that enchantment through a wet season, through a river crossing, through being buried in mud for a week, and delivers it every time it lands. It is not a spell in the field; it is a spell put into iron in a dry room at Gideon at leisure, and carried out by a man who need not understand a word of it.

I have said in three reports that the correct employment of a battle-mage in this province is not as a caster at all but as a smith, and that one wizard sitting in a room at Gideon for a fortnight could send a hundred enchanted blades out to the posts, and that this would do more for the Ninth than any number of us standing in the rain looking impressive.

The Office has thanked me for these reports on each occasion.

V. WHY I THINK IT HAS NOT WORKED, AND HERE I AM GIVING AN OPINION.

The province is wet, and it is close, and it is green, and none of the three is anything the schools have ever had to think about.

A wizard is an instrument of distance. Everything the craft is for happens at eighty paces, and the whole of a wizard's training is the management of a stretch of open air between himself and a man he intends to inconvenience. Give him that stretch of air and he is the most expensive soldier in the Empire and worth it. Take it away and he is a slow man in a robe with a knife he was never taught to use.

There is no stretch of open air in this province. There is reed, and there is leaf, and there is a green fog with things in it, and the sight lines at Gideon are shorter than the reach of a garrison bill.

So the wizard is put in the middle of the column where he can see nothing, and by the time he can see anything the auxiliaries have settled the matter with a spear, and after nine years of this a battle-mage discovers that he has become a man who enchants blades in a dry room, which is what I have been recommending in writing since my second year and doing in fact since my fourth.

VI. WHAT I WOULD SAY TO A YOUNG WIZARD POSTED HERE.

Learn shock and let the rest go. Do not argue about it and do not spend a year proving to yourself what I have spent nine years proving.

Buy your salts locally in small quantities and expect to lose them, and do not ever tell the Office how much you are spending of your own money, because I did and it has been entered against my allowance.

Enchant everything. Every blade in your file, every serjeant's blade in the depot, the officer's if he will let you have it. It is unglamorous and it is the only thing you will do here that a serjeant will remember you for.

And find a rootkeeper who will talk to you, and go and sit with them, and be prepared to sit for a long time and be told nothing. What they do is not sorcery in any sense the schools would accept, and it works in this country, and the Office has never in sixty years commissioned a single report on it, and I have applied twice.

VII. LAST.

I have been unattached for a year. The Cohort is polite to me and I dine well and no serjeant has asked me for anything since the spring.

I do not blame the province. It is a country with weather in it, and a craft that will not work in weather is a craft with a hole in it, and the hole was in my training before I ever saw a marsh.

I would have liked a wizard nine years ahead of me to have written this before I came. I looked for such a page in the depot library at Gideon when I arrived, and again in the Office library at Lilmoth, and neither of them had one. So I have written it, and the Office may file it with the applications.

books.title: The Chant of the Second Rank, As It Is Called at the Thorn Depot
books.author: traditional; the version here is Dag Ostrey's, taken down by the cohort clerk, and Ostrey says the last verse is not his
books.unreliability: A working chant that has been sung by men who were killed, so its cheerful arithmetic has been read as an omen by every recruit who has ever learned it. Ostrey disowns the last verse, which is the only verse anybody remembers, and 3 depots sing a different last verse each.
books.text:
*(Sung at the drill, slow, on the stroke, by the bill-men of the second rank. The serjeant calls the first line of each verse and the rank answers the rest. The rhythm is the haul, not the step.)*

Where's your eye?
On his knee, on his knee.
Where's your hook?
Under, under, under.
What d'you do?
Low. And pull.
Low. And pull.
Low. And pull.

Where's your mate?
In the front, in the front.
Who's he for?
Me, me, me.
